lesson.title: Fast answers: indexes
lesson.subtitle: Reading every row, halving with an index, and what it costs

video.title: Fast answers: indexes
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — the science teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph — the computer studies teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Icon cards: A million names; Page by page?; From the middle?. Mr Okafor beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Find one phone number in a city's phone book of a million names. Page by page? Or open it in the middle?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name and the lesson title with the Data engineering track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: why a database finds one row among millions so fast.

scenes.visual: One big value: 500,000, Looks, row by row, in a million rows.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Row by row: half the table
scenes.narration: Without help, a database reads row by row until it finds what you asked for. On average, that's half the table: five hundred thousand looks for a million rows.

scenes.visual: Numbered steps: Look at the middle; Too big? Drop the top half; Too small? Drop the bottom; Each look halves what's left.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: But if the ids are sorted, you can halve the search. Look at the middle: too big? Throw away the top half. Too small? Throw away the bottom. Each look halves what's left.

scenes.visual: Two columns: “Row by row” (500,000 looks) and “With an index” (About 20 looks).
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: An index is a sorted copy of one column, with a pointer to each row. For a million rows, halving takes about twenty looks, not half a million.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: lo, hi = 0, len(ids) - 1 … Caption: Each time round, half the list is ruled out
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Here's binary search in Python. lo and hi mark the part that's left. Each time round, look at the middle, and move lo or hi past it.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A million sorted ids. About how many looks does halving need to find one?

scenes.visual: One big value: 20, Looks to find one in a million.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: About twenty: two to the power of twenty is just over a million. Ten times more rows adds only about three more looks.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Each takes space; Every new row: slower; Index what you search by.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Indexes aren't free. Each one takes space, and every new row must be added to every index. So index the columns you search by, not every column.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: CREATE INDEX by_name … Caption: Now this WHERE uses the index
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In SQL, one line makes an index. Real databases use a tree that works like halving, with many branches, so even a billion rows take only a few steps.

scenes.visual: Icon cards joined by arrows: Watch one lookup; Grow to 1M rows; 500,000 vs 20.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: why an index is fast
scenes.narration: In the app, watch one lookup both ways, then grow the table to a million rows. Without an index, about half a million looks each; with one, about twenty.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Why not put an index on every column?

scenes.visual: Summary card: Row by row: half the table; An index halves the search; About 20 looks for a million; Space traded for speed. Takeaway bar: Sorted data can be searched by halves.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Each one costs space and slows every insert, so index what you search by. Remember: row by row takes half the table. A sorted index halves the search each time: about twenty looks for a million. And indexes trade space for speed.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Guess my number: 1 to 100; Always guess the middle; Seven guesses: why?. Mr Okafor beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: play “Guess my number” from one to a hundred with a friend. Always guess the middle. Can you always win in seven guesses? Why seven?

checkpoints.prompt: A million sorted ids: about how many looks does halving need to find one?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — each look halves what's left, and 2 to the power 20 is just over a million.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — halving a million twenty times leaves one: about 20 looks. 500,000 is reading row by row.

checkpoints.prompt: Why not put an index on every column?

options.text: Each index takes space and slows every new row

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — indexes trade space and slower writes for faster searches, so index what you search by.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — indexes don't change answers and you can have many. But each costs space and slows every insert.
